failure_summary.description: Treated a time-relative clue word (“current”) as present-day rather than considering the clue’s historical frame.
Selected a related answer from context without satisfying the clue’s full wordplay, rank progression, or requested role.
Identified the intended entity or term but returned an overextended name or a noncanonical spelling variant.

patch.reasoning: Add guidance for interpreting time-relative wording in historical clues. Refine the existing name-form guidance to resolve tension between expanding names and retaining conventional initials, and to reinforce minimal forms of address and canonical term spelling. The other target-resolution failures already match existing rules, so duplicating those rules is unlikely to help.

edits.target: Use the supported conventional name form: expand a nickname to the full given name when the evidence supports it, and omit optional middle initials or generational suffixes unless requested or needed to distinguish the person. Thus prefer Patricia Hearst, Lyndon Johnson, and Alan Shepard when those are the supported answer forms. Conversely, do not shorten a proper publication title by removing a word that belongs to it: when the journal is named Forbes magazine, return Forbes magazine rather than Forbes.
edits.content: Use the source-supported conventional answer form, not automatically the longest possible form or a merely equivalent variant. Expand a nickname only when the full given name is the conventional identifying form; retain established initials instead of expanding them to a disclosed middle name unless the full name is requested. Omit only genuinely optional, nonconventional initials or suffixes. If asked what someone is called, return the form of address itself without appending the person's name unless that is part of the appellation. Preserve conventional spelling, capitalization, and hyphenation. Retain every word that belongs to a proper title, as in “Forbes magazine.”

In historical or archival clues, interpret time-relative terms such as “current” or “now” relative to the clue’s source or publication date when that frame is identifiable; do not automatically substitute the present-day officeholder for the person intended by an older clue.
